---
title: "How fast is fasttrop?"
description: >
  Why speed matters for TROP, what makes fasttrop fast, and how to make your
  own runs faster.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
source("_setup.R")
bench <- function(file) {
  utils::read.csv(system.file("bench", file, package = "fasttrop"))
}
```

::: {.key-points}
Key points

- We wanted fasttrop to be fast, because one TROP analysis calculates
  thousands of fits.
- The model fits run in C, and they can use more than one thread. For a 20 by
  12 panel with fixed tuning parameters and no bootstrap, the R code added 0.8
  to 1.7 ms to each call.
- In our benchmarks with one thread and fixed tuning parameters, fasttrop was
  25 to 174 times faster than the Python packages. It was 136 to 152 times
  faster than an R package that uses only R code.
- The times depend on your computer.
:::

## Why speed matters

One TROP estimate is fast. The time goes to the steps around the estimate:

- The leave-one-out criterion calculates a new fit for each untreated cell
  that it uses, for each candidate value of the tuning parameters.
- The bootstrap calculates the full estimate again for each draw.
- The local method calculates a separate fit for each treated cell.

The example on the home page has 40 treated cells. Its cross-validation
examines 200 cells at each of 28 grid points. Its bootstrap calculates 200
more estimates. In total, the example calculates approximately 14,000 weighted
fits.

In our benchmark, one fit for a panel of this size took approximately 8 ms
with fasttrop on one thread. It took approximately 0.23 s with `diff-diff` in
Python. If we scale these times to 14,000 fits, the difference is
approximately 2 minutes against approximately one hour. This is a scale-up of
one benchmark, not a measured run of the example.

## What makes fasttrop fast

- All model fits are in C, in the file `src/trop_core.c`. The C code does not
  call R while it runs. R prepares the data, draws the samples, and calculates
  the standard error and the interval.
- Independent fits run on more than one thread at the same time, with OpenMP.
  The number of threads does not change the results.
- fasttrop uses the BLAS and LAPACK libraries of R. If R uses a faster BLAS
  library, fasttrop also uses it.
- The default solver is an accelerated method. It usually uses fewer of its
  most costly steps, the singular value decompositions, than the solver of the
  reference implementations.
- The fit for a cell starts from the solution for the previous cell of the
  same unit.

## A comparison with other implementations

We compared fasttrop with the other implementations of TROP on the same two
panels and with the same fixed tuning parameters. Each package used its
default solver options. The panels had 20 units and 15 periods, and 40 units
and 20 periods.

```{r speed-fig, fig.asp = 0.62, fig.cap = "How many times faster fasttrop with one thread was than each other implementation, on the same panels and with the same fixed tuning parameters. The leave-one-out criterion is one evaluation for all 284 untreated cells. The cfcompare bars are not exactly the same calculation, because its ATTs differed by up to 0.006. The authors' package has only the global method, and cfcompare has only the local method.", fig.alt = "A bar chart in three groups. For the global ATT, fasttrop was 31 and 25 times faster than the package of the authors, and 174 and 93 times faster than diff-diff. For the local ATT, it was 78 and 29 times faster than diff-diff, and 136 and 152 times faster than cfcompare. For one evaluation of the leave-one-out criterion, it was 66 times faster than diff-diff."}
ref <- bench("reference-timings.csv")
ref <- ref[!grepl("^fasttrop", ref$implementation), ]
ref$package <- sub(" \\(.*$", "", ref$implementation)
ref$package <- ifelse(ref$package == "trop", "Authors' trop", ref$package)
ref$task <- ifelse(grepl("^global", ref$task), "Global ATT",
                   ifelse(grepl("^local", ref$task), "Local ATT",
                          "Leave-one-out criterion"))
ref$task <- factor(ref$task, levels = c("Global ATT", "Local ATT",
                                        "Leave-one-out criterion"))
ref$panel <- sub("panel_", "", ref$panel)
ref$panel <- sub("x", " x ", ref$panel)
ref$label <- paste0(ref$package, ", ", ref$panel)
ref <- ref[order(ref$task, ref$package, ref$panel), ]
ref$label <- factor(ref$label, levels = rev(unique(ref$label)))
pkg_cols <- c("Authors' trop" = ft_col[["teal_dark"]], "diff-diff" = ft_col[["teal"]],
              "cfcompare" = ft_col[["coral"]])

ggplot(ref, aes(slower_than_fasttrop_1thread, label, fill = package)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.0f times", slower_than_fasttrop_1thread)),
            hjust = -0.1, size = 3.8) +
  facet_grid(task ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y", switch = "y",
             labeller = label_wrap_gen(width = 16)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pkg_cols, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.28))) +
  labs(x = "Times faster", y = NULL) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), strip.placement = "outside",
        strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 11))
```

| Task | Panel | fasttrop, 1 thread | fasttrop, 4 threads | Authors' `trop` | `diff-diff` | `cfcompare` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Local ATT | 20 x 15 | 0.044 s | 0.016 s | | 3.42 s | 5.93 s |
| Local ATT | 40 x 20 | 0.33 s | 0.088 s | | 9.33 s | 49.7 s |
| Global ATT | 20 x 15 | 0.0032 s | 0.0040 s | 0.100 s | 0.551 s | |
| Global ATT | 40 x 20 | 0.010 s | 0.0084 s | 0.252 s | 0.951 s | |
| One evaluation of the leave-one-out criterion, 284 cells | 20 x 15 | 0.85 s | 0.20 s | | 56.6 s | |

An empty cell shows that the package does not have the method. The ATTs of
fasttrop and the two Python packages had a difference of less than 1e-5. The
ATTs of `cfcompare` had a difference of up to 0.006. Thus, `cfcompare` does not
calculate exactly the same value. `diff-diff` ran in Python only, because its
optional Rust code was not available. With the Rust code, its times can be
shorter.

## R adds almost no time

To measure the cost of the R code, we wrote a C program that uses the same C
core as the package. The program runs the same calculations as R, with the
same sampled cells and the same bootstrap draws. Its results are the same as
the results of the package, bit for bit.

We examined the runs of one second or more. For these runs, the ratio of the R
time to the C time had a geometric mean of 1.012. Its 95% interval was 0.983
to 1.041. Thus, in the limits of the measurement, the package has the same
speed as a pure C program. For a 20 by 12 panel with fixed tuning parameters
and no bootstrap, the full R call added 0.8 to 1.7 ms in our benchmark. A call
with tuning or a bootstrap can add more R time.

## More threads

The table gives the time of the full R call with one thread and with four
threads, for four workloads. The values are medians of three rounds.

```{r threads}
res <- bench("results.csv")
res <- res[, c("config", "threads", "r_trop_matrix_s")]
wide <- reshape(res, idvar = "config", timevar = "threads", direction = "wide")
wide$speedup <- wide$r_trop_matrix_s.1 / wide$r_trop_matrix_s.4
pretty_s <- function(x) ifelse(x < 1, sprintf("%.3f s", x), sprintf("%.1f s", x))
tab <- data.frame(
  Workload = wide$config,
  `1 thread` = pretty_s(wide$r_trop_matrix_s.1),
  `4 threads` = pretty_s(wide$r_trop_matrix_s.4),
  `Times faster` = sprintf("%.1f", wide$speedup),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(tab, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"))
```

With four threads, each workload was
`r sprintf("%.1f to %.1f", min(wide$speedup), max(wide$speedup))` times faster
than with one thread. The times have some noise, so a value above 4 is
possible.

## How to make your runs faster

1. Use more threads. The default is the number of physical cores. To set it,
   use `trop_control(threads = 8)`.
2. Use a sample of cells for the leave-one-out criterion, for example
   `cv_cells = 200`. With `cv_cells = NULL`, the criterion uses all untreated
   cells. This uses all the data, but it takes more time.
3. Use a smaller grid of tuning parameters with `trop_grid()`.
4. When you explore the data, use fewer bootstrap draws, or `se = "none"`.
   For the final result, use more draws.
5. When you repeat an analysis with the same tuning parameters, set `lambda`.
   Then fasttrop does not run the cross-validation.

The global method is also faster, because it calculates one fit for all
treated cells. But it is a different estimator, and it works only for a block
design. Do not select it only for speed.

## Windows power throttling

Windows can use power throttling on a process that runs in the background for
a long time. This can make a long calculation in R slower. Thus, the threads
of fasttrop tell Windows not to use power throttling while the C code runs.
When the C code stops, Windows controls the threads again. To keep the usual
Windows policy, use `trop_control(throttle = TRUE)`. This option does not
change the results, and it has no effect on other operating systems.

## Your times can be different

The times on this page depend on the computer, the compiler, the BLAS library,
and the number of threads. Other work on the computer also changes the times.
All benchmarks used the reference BLAS and LAPACK libraries of R. The folder
`inst/bench` of the source package has the scripts, so you can measure the
times on your own computer.
